quiz.q: What was Thailand's Prevention of Animal Cruelty and Welfare Act 2014 the first to do?
options: Specifically criminalize animal cruelty in Thailand — no prior standalone law existed
Require all shelters to be government-funded
quiz.explanation: Thailand's 2014 Prevention of Animal Cruelty and Welfare Act was groundbreaking as the country's first standalone law specifically criminalizing animal cruelty. Prior to this Act, animal cruelty in Thailand was addressed only indirectly through other legal provisions.

laws.title: Thailand Civil and Commercial Code — Same-Sex Marriage 2024
laws.subtitle: Thailand became the first Southeast Asian country to legalize same-sex marriage in 2024
laws.fullDescription: Thailand enacted groundbreaking same-sex marriage legislation in 2024 — becoming the first country in Southeast Asia to do so. The Marriage Equality Act was approved by the Thai Senate in June 2024 and signed into law, effective January 2025. Thai family law is governed by the Civil and Commercial Code (CCC). Thailand's default property regime for married couples is community of property (sin somros). Divorce by agreement (withdrawal of registration) is available; contested divorce requires court. Child custody: Thai family courts prioritize children's welfare. Thailand had previously offered the Civil Partnership Bill as an alternative to same-sex marriage — the Marriage Equality Act superseded this, giving full marriage rights.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement through สำนักงานอัยการ (prosecutor's office) and courts; maintenance enforcement; criminal domestic violence charges under PDPA
exceptions: Pre-marital property (sin suan tua)
Premarital agreement (sanya haeng chep sapsin)
International marriages subject to dual registration
laws.sourceLabel: Thailand Civil and Commercial Code & Marriage Equality Act 2024

quiz.q: What historic milestone did Thailand achieve in 2024 regarding same-sex marriage?
options: Thailand became the second Asian country to legalize same-sex marriage
Thailand became the first Southeast Asian country to legalize same-sex marriage (effective January 2025)
Thailand allowed civil unions but not full marriage
Thailand legalized same-sex marriage by court ruling
quiz.explanation: Thailand's Marriage Equality Act (enacted 2024, effective January 2025) made Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to legalize same-sex marriage — a historic milestone in the region. The law grants same-sex couples full and equal marriage rights, setting an example for neighboring countries in Southeast Asia.

laws.title: Thailand Land Code & Condominium Act
laws.subtitle: Foreign ownership restrictions and condominium rules
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Land Code (1954, amended) restricts foreign nationals from owning land freehold. Foreigners can own condominium units up to 49% of building floor area under the Condominium Act (1979, amended 2008). Long-term leases (up to 30 years, renewable) are commonly used by foreigners as a land ownership workaround. The Thailand Elite Card program offers extended visa-linked leasehold rights. The 30-year lease is registered at the Land Department and can be mortgaged. Thai REITs (Trust for Real Property Investment) allow indirect foreign investment. Recently, the government has considered reforms to attract foreign property investment.
laws.penalty: Illegal foreign land ownership: confiscation; condominium quota violation: sale voidable
exceptions: 49% foreign condominium quota applies per building
30-year leases are maximum registerable land lease term
laws.source: Land Code BE 2497; Condominium Act BE 2522

quiz.q: What percentage of condominium floor area in Thailand can legally be owned by foreign nationals?
quiz.explanation: Thailand's Condominium Act allows foreigners to own up to 49% of the total floor area of any condominium building, with the remaining 51% required to be owned by Thai nationals, limiting foreign control of any single building.

laws.title: Thailand Consumer Protection Act & OCPB
laws.subtitle: Label, advertising, and product safety protections
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Consumer Protection Act (CPA, 1979, amended) protects consumers through mandatory labeling requirements, prohibition of false advertising, and product safety rules. The Office of the Consumer Protection Board (OCPB) enforces the law and receives public complaints. Thailand has specific laws for direct sales (Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act, 2002) with 20-day cooling-off period. Food and Drug Administration (FDA Thailand) regulates health product claims. Thailand's e-commerce sector has grown rapidly with Lazada and Shopee, creating new consumer protection challenges. The Electronic Transactions Act 2001 provides basic online consumer protections. Class actions for consumer harm were introduced in 2015.
laws.penalty: False advertising: fine up to THB 100,000 and criminal imprisonment up to 1 year; product recall authority
exceptions: 20-day cooling-off period for direct sales — longer than EU standard
Class actions for consumer protection introduced 2015
laws.source: Consumer Protection Act BE 2522 (1979); Direct Sales Act 2002

quiz.q: How does Thailand's cooling-off period for direct sales compare to the EU standard?
options: It matches the EU at 14 days
quiz.explanation: Thailand's Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act provides a 20-day cooling-off period for direct sales contracts — significantly longer than the EU's 14-day minimum and longer than most countries, giving Thai consumers extra time to reconsider direct sales purchases.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติประกอบรัฐธรรมนูญ — Constitutional Monarchy Law
laws.subtitle: Thailand's unique constitutional framework under royal governance
laws.fullDescription: Thailand has had 20 constitutions since 1932 — the most of any nation — reflecting its pattern of military coups (at least 19 since 1932) followed by new constitutional drafting. The current constitution (2017) was drafted after the 2014 military coup by General Prayuth Chan-o-cha. Key feature: an unelected Senate (appointed by military junta) had power for 5 years to vote in the Prime Minister alongside the elected lower house. The monarchy plays a central role: King Vajiralongkorn (Rama X) has significant formal powers including personal ownership of Crown Property Bureau assets (estimated $30-60 billion). Thailand's constitutional structure oscillates between democratic and quasi-military governance.
laws.penalty: Lèse-majesté (Section 112 Criminal Code): insulting the King, Queen, heir apparent, or regent — up to 15 years per count. Multiple counts have resulted in sentences of 43+ years.
exceptions: Parliament may debate issues touching on monarchy in 'confidential session'
Academic study of monarchy is nominally protected but practically sensitive
Foreign diplomats have immunity for statements in their official capacity

quiz.q: How many constitutions has Thailand had since 1932, reflecting its pattern of military coups?
options: 3 constitutions — similar to most stable democracies
20 constitutions — the most of any nation
quiz.explanation: Thailand has adopted 20 constitutions since 1932 — the highest number of any country — reflecting at least 19 military coups that each typically triggered a new constitutional framework. Each coup-installed government drafts a constitution favoring military oversight, which is then replaced after democratic transitions, until the next coup. This cycle makes Thailand's constitutional history uniquely turbulent.

laws.title: ประมวลกฎหมายอาญา มาตรา 112 — Lèse-Majesté Law
laws.subtitle: Thailand's severe penalties for criticizing the monarchy
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Criminal Code Section 112 criminalizes defaming, insulting, or threatening the King, Queen, heir apparent, or regent. The law has been applied to social media posts, academic articles, and performances. Crucially, any person can file a complaint — police must investigate, and prosecutors rarely dismiss. Maximum penalty is 15 years per count; multiple counts have resulted in 43+ year sentences. The 2020-21 pro-democracy protests, which included unprecedented calls for monarchy reform, led to mass Section 112 prosecutions. Bail is frequently denied. The UN, EU, and international human rights organizations have repeatedly called for repeal or major reform.
laws.penalty: Insulting or defaming monarchy: 3 to 15 years imprisonment per count. Multiple posts or statements = multiple counts. Bail frequently refused making accused experience pre-trial imprisonment.
exceptions: Truthful statements are NOT a defense — unlike in defamation in democratic systems
Court proceedings discussing evidence are confidential to prevent further spread
Foreign nationals outside Thailand may still be prosecuted if they visit Thailand
laws.sourceLabel: iLaw — Internet Law Reform Dialogue Thailand

quiz.q: What makes Thailand's lèse-majesté law (Section 112) unusually severe compared to similar laws elsewhere?
options: It applies to the entire royal family including distant cousins
Any person can file a complaint requiring police investigation, multiple posts = multiple counts with no truth defense
It carries the death penalty in extreme cases
It applies retroactively to statements made before the law existed
quiz.explanation: Section 112 is unusually severe because: (1) any person can file a complaint — police must investigate, (2) there is no truth defense, (3) each social media post constitutes a separate count (so 100 posts = potentially 1,500 years maximum), and (4) bail is frequently refused. Compare this to European royal defamation laws that are rarely used and carry minor penalties.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติอาวุธปืน — Firearms Act
laws.subtitle: Gun laws and organized crime in Thailand
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Firearms Act (1947) requires licenses for all firearms. Thailand has relatively high gun ownership for Asia (approximately 10-15 per 100 people) — driven by rural self-defense culture. Organized crime (including political violence) has made 'hit-man' contract killings a persistent problem. The 2020 Korat mass shooting — a soldier killed 29 people at a mall — highlighted issues with military firearms access. Thailand has a significant problem with informal/homemade firearms (เครื่องกระสุน or 'ghost guns') in the deep south conflict zone. The restive southern provinces (Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat) have experienced a Malay-Muslim insurgency since 2004 with 7,000+ deaths.
laws.penalty: Carrying a licensed firearm in public without permission: up to 1 year imprisonment. Illegal possession of unlicensed firearm: up to 10 years. Using a firearm in a crime: enhanced sentences.
exceptions: Licensed sport shooters may transport firearms to ranges
Security guards with employer-sponsored licenses may carry while on duty
Military and police personnel carry under separate regulations

quiz.q: What armed conflict has caused 7,000+ deaths in Thailand's southern provinces since 2004?
options: A Cold War-era communist insurgency continuing from the 1960s
A Malay-Muslim separatist insurgency in Pattani, Yala, and Narathiwat provinces
A drug cartel conflict along the Myanmar border
An ethnic Hmong independence movement in the north
quiz.explanation: A Malay-Muslim insurgency in Thailand's three southernmost provinces (Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat) has caused 7,000+ deaths since it reignited in 2004. The region has a historically distinct identity — formerly part of the Pattani Sultanate — and indigenous language (Malay dialect) and religion (Islam) different from Buddhist Thai majority. The conflict, involving bombings, assassinations, and school attacks, receives little international attention despite its scale.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติว่าด้วยการกระทำความผิดเกี่ยวกับคอมพิวเตอร์ — Computer Crimes Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's internet controls and online speech restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Computer Crimes Act (2007, amended 2017) criminalizes hacking, malware, and online fraud, but also broadly prohibits content 'affecting national security', 'causing public panic', or 'disturbing public order'. Section 14 on false or distorted computer data has been widely used against political critics. Thailand has used internet blocking orders extensively: websites critical of the monarchy, political opposition sites, and pornography. A ministerial committee can block websites without court order for national security. Social media platforms including Facebook and Twitter have complied with Thai government content removal requests, though sometimes resisting specific demands.
laws.penalty: Uploading false data causing damage to third party: up to 5 years imprisonment. Content affecting national security: up to 5 years. Unauthorized access to computer system: up to 2 years.
exceptions: Legitimate security research with authorization of system owner
Government agencies accessing systems within their mandate
Ordinary encryption and security software use by individuals

quiz.q: What makes Thailand's Computer Crimes Act controversial beyond its cybercrime provisions?
options: It prohibits Thais from using VPNs or foreign-hosted email services
Section 14 on false computer data has been used broadly against political critics and regime opponents
It requires all websites to be hosted on Thai servers
It mandates government access to all encrypted communications
quiz.explanation: Thailand's CCA is controversial primarily because Section 14, meant to address fraud and false information online, has been interpreted broadly to prosecute political critics, opposition activists, and people sharing news critical of the government or monarchy. The 2017 amendments were criticized as further expanding censorship powers rather than focusing on genuine cybercrime.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองแรงงาน — Labour Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Worker rights and migrant labor in Thailand
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Labour Protection Act (1998) sets minimum standards for working hours (8/day, 48/week), paid leave (annual leave after 1 year, minimum 6 days), and statutory public holidays. Thailand's minimum wage varies by province (highest in Bangkok: ~370 baht/day ≈ $10). A critical issue is migrant labor: Thailand hosts 4-5 million documented migrant workers (primarily from Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos) who are legally entitled to the same protections as Thai workers but face exploitation, document confiscation, and debt bondage — particularly in fishing, garment, and domestic work. Thailand received US Tier 3 (worst) rating for human trafficking before improvements.
laws.penalty: Non-payment of wages: criminal prosecution plus double-pay liability. Child labor under 15: 1 year imprisonment and ¥20,000 fine. Exploitation of workers: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Domestic workers in private homes have limited LPA protections — separate ministerial regulation applies
Agricultural workers partially exempt from certain provisions
Family businesses employing only family members exempt
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Labour — Royal Thai Government

quiz.q: What human trafficking vulnerability exists in Thailand's fishing industry?
options: Thailand's fishing boats export all catch to human trafficking destination countries
Migrant workers on fishing vessels face document confiscation, debt bondage, and violence far from shore
Thai fishing companies only employ domestic workers making labor abuses impossible
Fish caught by trafficked labor is prohibited from US markets
quiz.explanation: Thailand's deep-sea fishing industry has been documented as a site of severe labor abuse: migrant workers (often Burmese or Cambodian) lured by false promises, have documents confiscated, work in debt bondage on vessels far from shore where escape is impossible, and face violence. The US placed Thailand on its Tier 3 human trafficking watch list (worst tier) before Thailand took steps to improve monitoring and prosecution of traffickers.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติธุรกิจของคนต่างด้าว — Foreign Business Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's restrictions on foreign business ownership
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Foreign Business Act (1999) restricts or prohibits foreigners from operating in many sectors. List 1 (absolutely prohibited): media, farming, forestry, fishing, land ownership, antiques. List 2 (require Cabinet approval): certain services, transportation, domestic trade in indigenous products. List 3 (require Department of Business Development approval): retail, wholesale, construction, accounting, advertising, tourism. Foreigners are typically limited to 49% ownership in restricted businesses. Many foreign investors use Thai nominee shareholders (อำพรางความเป็นเจ้าของ) — technically illegal but widespread. The BOI (Board of Investment) offers tax incentives and majority ownership rights in certain promoted industries.
laws.penalty: Operating restricted business without license: up to 3 years imprisonment and ฿1M fine. Using Thai nominees to circumvent FBA: criminal prosecution of both parties.
exceptions: BOI-promoted companies may receive foreign majority ownership in promoted activities
Treaty of Amity (US-Thailand) allows US citizens majority ownership in most sectors
Free Trade Zone businesses have modified foreign ownership restrictions

quiz.q: What legal mechanism do many foreign investors use to circumvent Thailand's 49% foreign ownership limit, despite being technically illegal?
options: Creating a holding company in Singapore to qualify as ASEAN investment
Using Thai nominee shareholders who hold shares on paper while the foreigner retains effective control
Registering as a BOI-promoted company in all sectors
Applying for a special Foreign Business License available to all investors
quiz.explanation: Thai nominee shareholders (Thai citizens holding company shares 'on paper' while a foreigner has effective economic control through side agreements) are technically prohibited under the Foreign Business Act and associated laws. Despite this, the practice is widespread — a significant grey area in Thai business law. Enforcement has been episodic rather than systematic, though individual prosecutions do occur.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติส่งเสริมและรักษาคุณภาพสิ่งแวดล้อม — Enhancement and Conservation of National Environmental Quality Act
laws.subtitle: Environmental protection in Thailand including marine and forest
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Enhancement and Conservation of National Environmental Quality Act (NEQA, 1992) provides the framework for environmental protection. Thailand's environmental challenges are significant: plastic pollution in the Gulf of Thailand, coral bleaching, mangrove destruction for aquaculture shrimp ponds (50%+ of mangroves lost), and air pollution from agricultural burning in the north. The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration implements city-specific environmental rules. Coral reef protection around Koh Tao and other dive sites has been strengthened. Thailand joined the Global Plastics Treaty negotiations and has domestic plastic bag bans at major retail stores (since 2020).
laws.penalty: Pollution causing public health damage: up to 5 years imprisonment and ฿1M fine. Illegal logging: up to 20 years imprisonment under Forest Act. Illegal wildlife trade: up to 4 years.
exceptions: Small-scale traditional fishing may have modified marine conservation requirements
Tourism operators in national marine parks must comply with marine conservation requirements
Agricultural burning seasonally permitted under specific conditions in some provinces
laws.sourceLabel: Office of Natural Resources and Environmental Policy and Planning

quiz.q: What major environmental transformation happened to Thailand's mangrove forests?
options: Mangroves expanded significantly due to reforestation programs
Over 50% of Thailand's mangroves were destroyed for shrimp aquaculture ponds
Thailand banned all coastal development to protect mangroves
Mangroves were classified as protected forest in 1985 before any significant loss
quiz.explanation: Thailand lost over 50% of its mangrove forests primarily to conversion for commercial shrimp aquaculture ponds — intensive shrimp farming that generates export income but destroys crucial coastal ecosystems. Mangroves provide hurricane protection, fish nurseries, carbon storage, and coastal erosion prevention. Thailand has since implemented mangrove restoration programs, but recovering destroyed mangrove ecosystems takes decades.

laws.title: ประมวลกฎหมายที่ดิน — Land Code — Foreign Land Ownership
laws.subtitle: Thailand's prohibition on foreign land ownership
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Land Code prohibits foreigners from owning land outright. Foreigners can: own condominium units up to 49% of total building floor area, hold 30-year leases (renewable for up to 90 years), use company structures (with Thai majority ownership), or invest ฿40M+ to qualify for limited land ownership (maximum 1 rai = 0.4 acres). The Royal Decree of 2022 sought to attract long-term residents: foreigners investing $1M+ in Thai bonds/real estate qualify for special long-term resident status with modified property rules. Proximity to foreigners and retirees moving to Thailand has created a large market for foreign property ownership work-arounds.
laws.penalty: Foreigners illegally holding land: land forfeiture. Thai nationals holding land as nominees for foreigners: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: BOI-promoted companies with 51% Thai ownership can own land for business operations
Foreigners receiving land through inheritance may hold it for up to 1 year before disposal
Foreign governments and international organizations may own diplomatic premises
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Lands — Royal Thai Government

quiz.q: What is the maximum condominium ownership percentage available to foreigners in a Thai building?
options: No limit — foreigners can own 100% of a condo building
49% of total floor space in a condominium project — protecting Thai majority in any building
Foreigners cannot own any real estate in Thailand, only long-term leases
quiz.explanation: Thailand allows foreigners to own condominium units, but total foreign ownership cannot exceed 49% of a building's total floor area. This means if a building is already 49% foreign-owned, no more units can be sold to foreigners — protecting Thai majority ownership in every building. This is the only form of direct real property ownership permitted to foreigners without special investment visa status.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติควบคุมการแลกเปลี่ยนเงิน — Exchange Control Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's currency controls and capital flow management
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Exchange Control Act (1942, extensively amended) regulates currency exchange and capital flows. The Bank of Thailand (BoT) maintains moderate capital controls: residents may send up to $1M abroad per year without special approval, foreign investors may freely repatriate profits. Thailand learned painful lessons from the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis — when the Thai baht's collapse triggered the regional crisis after speculative attacks exposed the unsustainable dollar peg. Since then, Thailand has maintained managed float exchange rate. Foreign currency accounts are permitted. Cryptocurrency is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission as digital assets.
laws.penalty: Violation of exchange control regulations: up to 3 years imprisonment and ฿2M fine. Undeclared import/export of currency exceeding THB 450,000: confiscation.
exceptions: Tourism-related foreign currency exchange freely permitted at licensed exchangers
Multinational corporations with BoT approval may netting cross-border intercompany transactions
ASEAN members may settle trade in local currencies under ASEAN FX framework

quiz.q: What 1997 event involving Thailand's currency had global financial consequences?
options: Thailand revalued its currency upward, disrupting Asian exports
The Thai baht's collapse under speculative attack triggered the Asian Financial Crisis affecting multiple countries
Thailand banned all foreign exchange trading, causing market seizure
The Thai central bank accidentally printed 10 times normal money supply
quiz.explanation: In July 1997, Thailand was forced to abandon its dollar peg after sustained speculative attacks depleted foreign currency reserves. The baht collapsed, triggering cascading currency crises in Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, and the Philippines — the Asian Financial Crisis. Thailand required a $17 billion IMF bailout. The crisis led many Asian countries to build massive foreign currency reserves as protection against future speculative attacks.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติยาเสพติดให้โทษ — Narcotics Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's drug laws and recent cannabis decriminalization
laws.fullDescription: Thailand has strict drug laws: methamphetamine (ya ba, ยาบ้า) trafficking carries the death penalty. Thailand is on the Mekong 'Golden Triangle' border with Myanmar's Shan State drug production. However, Thailand made groundbreaking moves: it became the first Asian country to legalize medical cannabis in 2018 and removed cannabis from the narcotics list in 2022 — allowing home cultivation and commercial sale. This led to a cannabis tourism boom. However, the incoming conservative government in 2023 announced intentions to re-criminalize recreational cannabis while maintaining medical use. Kratom (กระท่อม, Mitragyna speciosa) — a traditional stimulant — was also decriminalized in 2021.
laws.penalty: Death penalty: trafficking more than 20g pure heroin or 375g+ amphetamines. Life imprisonment: manufacturing or importing hard drugs. Cannabis: legalized for medicinal/personal use but recreational re-criminalization proposed.
exceptions: Licensed cannabis dispensaries and medical users legally operate
Kratom decriminalized — traditional chewing and tea consumption legal
Traditional healers may use traditional medicinal preparations including scheduled plants
laws.sourceLabel: Office of the Narcotics Control Board — Thailand

quiz.q: What made Thailand historically groundbreaking in Asian drug policy in 2022?
options: Thailand became the first Asian country to decriminalize all drug possession
Thailand removed cannabis from its narcotics list — the first Asian country to do so — allowing home cultivation and commercial sale
Thailand abolished the death penalty for all drug offenses
Thailand created the first Asian government-owned cannabis pharmaceutical company
quiz.explanation: In June 2022, Thailand removed cannabis from the narcotics list — the first Asian country to effectively decriminalize cannabis, allowing home cultivation of up to 6 plants and commercial cannabis businesses. This created a cannabis tourism boom with thousands of dispensaries opening quickly. However, the conservative government elected in 2023 signaled intent to re-criminalize recreational use while maintaining medical legalization.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติคนเข้าเมือง — Immigration Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's visa system and management of tourists and expats
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Immigration Act regulates entry and residence of foreigners. Thailand is a major tourism destination (40M+ tourists pre-COVID) and popular expat destination (around 100,000 Western expats). Thailand has a complex visa system: tourist visa (60 days, extendable), retirement visa (Non-OA, requiring ฿800,000 in Thai bank), education visa, business visa. 'Visa runs' — leaving Thailand briefly to renew tourist stays — have been restricted. The long-term resident (LTR) visa introduced in 2022 offers 10-year renewable visas to wealthy foreigners ($80,000+/year income), remote workers, and highly skilled professionals with a 4-year tax on foreign income.
laws.penalty: Overstaying visa: ฿500/day fine (capped at ฿20,000), deportation, and re-entry ban. Working on tourist visa: up to 5 years imprisonment for foreigner, criminal liability for employer.
exceptions: ASEAN citizens receive 30-day visa-free entry
Permanent residents have unlimited right to reside
Thai sufficiency economy visa for skilled retirees has modified financial requirements

quiz.q: What is the financial requirement for a Thailand retirement (Non-OA) visa?
options: No financial requirement — just proof of age 50+
฿800,000 (~$22,000) deposited in a Thai bank account, or monthly income/pension of ฿65,000+
Proof of pension income equivalent to Thai minimum wage
Property ownership in Thailand valued at ฿3,000,000+
quiz.explanation: Thailand's retirement visa (Non-OA) requires either ฿800,000 (~$22,000) deposited in a Thai bank account throughout the visa period, or monthly pension/income of at least ฿65,000. The money must remain in a Thai bank — it cannot be withdrawn below the threshold. This financial requirement has been criticized as excluding retirees with adequate foreign pensions who dislike parking money in Thailand.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติกฎอัยการศึก — Martial Law Act
laws.subtitle: Military power invocations in Thailand
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Martial Law Act allows the military to declare martial law — which has been used extensively given Thailand's 19+ coups. The 2014 coup by General Prayuth Chan-o-cha began with martial law declaration, then became a coup under the National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO). Under NCPO rule (2014-2019), criticism of the junta was criminalized, political gatherings of 5+ people prohibited, and dissidents summoned for 'attitude adjustment'. NCPO used its Article 44 power (equivalent to martial law decree power) to issue executive orders bypassing all legislative and judicial review. The 2017 constitution allowed NCPO-appointed senators to participate in PM selection for 5 years — allowing the junta leader to become PM through 'democratic' election.
laws.penalty: Disobeying military orders during martial law: criminal prosecution. Violations of NCPO orders: criminal prosecution. Challenge to martial law declaration: not possible through normal legal channels.
exceptions: Civil courts may still operate for non-security matters during limited martial law
Religious activities generally not subject to martial law restrictions
International obligations under Vienna Convention maintained for diplomats

quiz.q: How did Thailand's 2014 coup leader General Prayuth transition from military ruler to elected Prime Minister?
options: He won a fair election by popular vote in 2019
The 2017 constitution allowed junta-appointed senators to vote in PM selection — allowing him to win without majority popular vote
He was appointed PM by the King as a royal prerogative
He retired from military, joined a party, and won a democratic primary
quiz.explanation: Thailand's 2017 constitution, drafted under junta control, included a transitional provision allowing 250 unelected senators (all NCPO-appointed) to vote alongside elected MPs in selecting the PM for the first 5 years. In 2019 elections, although Pheu Thai won most popular votes, Prayuth was re-elected PM through the combined elected house + junta-appointed senate vote — allowing unelected military nominees to determine the government.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติหลักประกันสุขภาพแห่งชาติ — National Health Security Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's universal healthcare system: a model for developing nations
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Universal Health Coverage scheme (บัตรทอง, Gold Card, 2002) is considered one of the most successful universal healthcare implementations in a middle-income country. It covers 48+ million Thais not covered by civil servant or social security insurance. For a ฿30 co-pay per visit (now often free), patients access comprehensive care including outpatient, inpatient, surgery, dialysis, ARV for HIV, and cancer treatment. Thailand achieves health outcomes comparable to much richer nations at much lower cost — sometimes called the 'Thai model'. International medical tourism brings billions: private hospitals in Bangkok compete with Singapore and South Korea for high-value patients.
laws.penalty: Healthcare fraud against NHSO: criminal prosecution. Private hospitals must follow NHSO pricing for emergency care regardless of patient insurance status.
exceptions: Civil servants use Civil Servant Medical Benefit Scheme (CSMBS) — more generous
Formal private sector employees covered by Social Security Office (SSO) scheme
Emergency care must be provided by any hospital — patient transferred or costs reimbursed later

quiz.q: What made Thailand's Universal Health Coverage scheme a model for developing nations?
options: Thailand achieved universal health coverage without any government funding
Comprehensive healthcare with very low co-pays (฿30 per visit, now often free) achieving rich-country health outcomes at middle-income cost
Thailand outsourced all healthcare to private companies achieving efficiency
Thailand's healthcare is only for tourists — locals use traditional medicine
quiz.explanation: Thailand's Gold Card scheme (2002) is studied globally as evidence that universal health coverage is achievable in middle-income countries. By pooling purchasing power and setting prices, Thailand provides comprehensive care — including expensive treatments like dialysis and cancer therapy — for all citizens at very low cost. Thailand's health outcomes (life expectancy, maternal mortality, HIV treatment rates) approach high-income country levels despite modest GDP per capita.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติส่งเสริมการลงทุน — Investment Promotion Act
laws.subtitle: Board of Investment incentives driving Thailand's industrial development
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Investment Promotion Act (1977) established the Board of Investment (BOI) — the flagship agency for attracting foreign direct investment. BOI incentives include: corporate income tax holidays (up to 13 years), no import duties on machinery, no import duties on raw materials for export production, and permission for foreign majority ownership in promoted activities. Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) — a special economic zone covering Chonburi, Rayong, and Chachoengsao provinces — offers enhanced incentives for 12 targeted industries including electric vehicles, aerospace, medical devices, and advanced manufacturing. Thailand aims to be an EV hub: government targets 30% EV production by 2030.
laws.penalty: Misuse of BOI privileges: revocation of BOI certificate and recovery of all tax benefits received. False declarations in BOI applications: criminal fraud prosecution.
exceptions: BOI-promoted companies may own land for business operations (normally prohibited for foreigners)
BOI executives may work without additional work permits
Promoted activities in special economic zones receive enhanced incentives beyond standard BOI

quiz.q: What is Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) strategy targeting?
options: Converting Eastern Thailand to organic agricultural production
A special economic zone targeting 12 advanced industries including EV manufacturing, with a goal of 30% EV production by 2030
Moving Thailand's capital from Bangkok to the east coast
Developing Eastern Thailand as the region's premier financial center
quiz.explanation: Thailand's EEC covers three eastern provinces and provides enhanced investment incentives to attract advanced manufacturing — particularly targeting electric vehicles, aerospace, medical devices, and digital industries. Thailand aims to position itself as Southeast Asia's EV manufacturing hub, with the government targeting 30% of domestic vehicle production to be electric by 2030 and attracting major investments from BYD, SAIC, and other Chinese EV makers.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติประกอบรัฐธรรมนูญว่าด้วยพรรคการเมือง — Political Parties Act
laws.subtitle: Dissolution of political parties in Thailand
laws.fullDescription: Thailand has a notable history of judicial dissolution of political parties. The Constitutional Court has dissolved: Thai Rak Thai (2007, 111 executive banned), Palang Prachachon (2008), Democrat Party case dismissed, Thai Raksa Chart (2019, nominated Princess Ubonratana for PM violating royal tradition), and Future Forward/Move Forward (2020, 2024 — for policy platform deemed threatening to constitutional monarchy). Move Forward's dissolution in 2024, after winning the most seats in 2023 elections, and banning of its leader Pita Limjaroenrat for 10 years, prompted international criticism about weaponization of constitutional law against popular opposition parties.
laws.penalty: Party dissolution orders: party ceases to exist. Executives of dissolved parties: 10-year ban on political participation. Continuance of banned activities: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Rank-and-file party members not banned — may join successor parties
Party assets do not automatically go to state — handled under party dissolution orders
Member of Parliament who was party member continues serving until next election

quiz.q: What happened to Thailand's Move Forward Party after winning the most seats in the 2023 election?
options: It formed a coalition government and implemented its platform
It was dissolved by the Constitutional Court in 2024 for its policy platform, and its leader was banned from politics for 10 years
It was allowed to govern only after removing its monarchy reform platform
It voluntarily dissolved after failing to form a coalition
quiz.explanation: Move Forward won the most seats in Thailand's May 2023 election on a platform including reform of the lèse-majesté law. It was blocked from forming government by junta-appointed senators. Then in 2024, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party for its monarchy reform platform (deemed threatening to the constitutional monarchy) and banned leader Pita Limjaroenrat from politics for 10 years — the latest in a series of judicial dissolutions of popular opposition parties.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติสงวนและคุ้มครองสัตว์ป่า — Wildlife Preservation and Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting Thailand's wildlife including domesticated elephants
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Wildlife Preservation and Protection Act (2019) lists 1,000+ protected wild species. Thailand is a major transit point for illegal wildlife trade — the region's proximity to China (largest consumer of wildlife products) drives demand. Tigers are critically endangered; Thailand's Tiger Temple scandal (2016) found 40 dead tiger cubs in freezers. Thai elephants have unique status: domestic (captive) elephants are classified as 'working animals' (livestock), not protected wildlife — creating legal grey areas for elephant camps and tourism. Wild elephants are protected. The ivory trade ban has been tightened but enforcement challenges remain.
laws.penalty: Killing protected species: up to 10 years and ฿1M fine. Wildlife trafficking: up to 15 years. Possession of protected species: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Traditional Thai medicine using protected plant species has modified provisions
Captive domestic elephants (non-wild) regulated under different livestock framework
Zoos and accredited sanctuaries may hold protected species under license
laws.sourceLabel: Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation

quiz.q: What legal anomaly exists in Thailand regarding elephants?
options: All elephants are royal property and cannot be privately owned
Domestic (captive) elephants are classified as livestock, not protected wildlife — creating different legal rules from wild elephants
Elephants may only be owned by Thai Buddhist temples
Foreign ownership of any elephants is prohibited
quiz.explanation: Thailand's unique legal system creates a two-tier elephant framework: wild elephants are protected wildlife under conservation law, while domestic (captive) elephants are classified as 'working animals' or livestock — historically used in logging and now in tourism. This means elephant camps operate under livestock laws (much less protective), while mahouts and camp operators need to manage the complex boundary between domesticated and wild legal status.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติป้องกันและปราบปรามการค้ามนุษย์ — Anti-Human Trafficking Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's human trafficking laws and enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Anti-Human Trafficking Act (2008) criminalizes trafficking for labor, sexual exploitation, and organ harvesting. Thailand is a source, transit, and destination country for trafficking: Burmese, Cambodian, and Lao workers trafficked into fishing, agriculture, and domestic work; women and girls trafficked into sex tourism. The US State Department's Trafficking in Persons Report placed Thailand on Tier 3 (worst) in 2014, citing deep-sea fishing slave labor. Thailand was upgraded to Tier 2 Watch List after implementing reforms: vessel monitoring, inspection of fishing fleets, labor inspectors on boats. Sex tourism, while nominally illegal, persists in 'entertainment' areas.
laws.penalty: Human trafficking: 4 to 20 years imprisonment and ฿400,000 to ฿2M fine. Trafficking for organ harvesting: 4 to 20 years. Officials complicit in trafficking: enhanced sentences.
exceptions: Voluntary sex work in licensed entertainment venues exists in legal grey area
Migrant workers with valid work permits and contracts distinguishable from trafficking victims
Refugee status provides protection against criminal prosecution for illegal entry
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Social Development and Human Security Thailand

quiz.q: What specific industry practice led the US to place Thailand on its worst-tier (Tier 3) human trafficking list in 2014?
options: Child labor in garment factories supplying US brands
Slave labor on deep-sea fishing vessels — workers trafficked and held captive on boats far from shore
Sex trafficking of women from neighboring countries
Organ harvesting operations linked to illegal clinics
quiz.explanation: The US Tier 3 designation in 2014 was specifically triggered by documented evidence of slave labor on Thailand's deep-sea fishing vessels: workers, primarily Burmese, were trafficked onto boats, had documents confiscated, and were held for months or years at sea unable to escape. The fish they caught entered Thailand's seafood export supply chain. After reforms — vessel monitoring, at-sea inspections, labor licensing — Thailand was upgraded, though concerns remain.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติธุรกิจสถาบันการเงิน — Financial Institution Business Act
laws.subtitle: Thai banking regulation and the Bank of Thailand
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Financial Institution Business Act (2008) governs commercial banks, finance companies, and credit institutions. The Bank of Thailand (BoT) acts as both central bank and banking regulator. Thailand's banking sector is dominated by Thai-owned banks: Bangkok Bank, Kasikorn Bank (KBank), SCB, and Krungthai Bank (government-owned). Foreign bank branches are permitted but limited. Thai banks have strong capital ratios following lessons from the 1997 crisis. Thailand's PromptPay system — launched 2017 — enables free instant transfers using national ID or phone number; over 60 million registered users. FinTech regulation is handled by BoT and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed financial institution: up to 5 years imprisonment. Bank directors facilitating fraud: criminal prosecution. Failure to maintain required capital ratios: regulatory intervention.
exceptions: Government savings banks (Government Savings Bank, BAAC) operate under separate legislation
Microfinance institutions (nanofinance) for low-income borrowers have modified rules
ASEAN banks from member countries benefit from ASEAN Banking Integration Framework

quiz.q: What free payment service did Thailand launch in 2017 that achieved 60 million user registrations?
options: ThaiPay — a government cryptocurrency for domestic transactions
PromptPay — instant free transfers using national ID or phone number
BlueCard — a government debit card for social welfare payments
KhunKhak — a contactless payment system for street markets
quiz.explanation: PromptPay, launched in 2017, allows free instant transfers between any Thai bank using just a national ID number or phone number — no account details needed. With 60+ million registered users (nearly Thailand's entire adult population), it has dramatically reduced cash usage and enabled efficient government payments (emergency stimulus, tax refunds). Thailand's real-time payment infrastructure is considered among the most advanced in Southeast Asia.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติการพัฒนาดิจิทัลเพื่อเศรษฐกิจและสังคม — Digital Economy and Society Act
laws.subtitle: Thailand's digital transformation framework and cybersecurity
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Digital Economy and Society Act (2016) established the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES) to drive Thailand's digital transformation. Thailand's National Cybersecurity Act (2019) created the National Cybersecurity Agency (NCSA) and National Cybersecurity Committee, and established incident reporting requirements for critical infrastructure operators. Thailand has a 'Thailand 4.0' vision for economic transition from agriculture and manufacturing to innovation-driven growth. Digital ID (Digital ID) and government services digitization are ongoing. Thailand's e-government ranking has improved. But cybercrime remains significant: call-center scam operations based across the border in Myanmar target Thai (and Chinese) victims.
laws.penalty: Critical infrastructure cyberattacks: up to 10 years imprisonment. Personal data breach without notification: up to ฿5M fine. Online fraud: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Licensed penetration testing and security research with system owner authorization
Authorized government intelligence activities on networks within their mandate
Academic cybersecurity research within ethical guidelines
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Digital Economy and Society Thailand

quiz.q: What cross-border cybercrime problem significantly affects Thailand and China?
options: Cryptocurrency mining farms illegally connected to Thai electrical grid
Call-center scam operations based in Myanmar using Thai and Chinese nationals as targets
Hacking of Thai government databases by foreign state actors
Online casino operations using servers in Thailand to serve Chinese gamblers
quiz.explanation: Large-scale call-center scam operations based in special economic zones in Myanmar (particularly in areas controlled by armed groups near Thai and Chinese borders) target victims in Thailand and China. Thai nationals are trafficked into these compounds as scam operators; Chinese nationals are also major targets. The compounds exploit Myanmar's governance gaps. Thailand has worked with Myanmar and China on law enforcement responses, though progress has been limited.

laws.title: พระราชบัญญัติการปฏิรูปที่ดินเพื่อเกษตรกรรม — Agricultural Land Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Land reform and rural tenure security in Thailand
laws.fullDescription: Thailand's Agricultural Land Reform Act (1975) established the Agricultural Land Reform Office (ALRO) to distribute land to poor farmers. Thailand's rural land tenure system has multiple title types with different legal security: Chanote (โฉนดที่ดิน, full title, most secure), Nor Sor 3 Gor (right to apply for full title), Sor Por Kor 4-01 (ALRO land — cannot be sold, only inherited, only farmed). ALRO land given to poor farmers cannot be sold to prevent reconcentration by wealthy buyers, but this also prevents farmers from using it as loan collateral — limiting investment in land. Thai farmers face increasing debt burdens and land consolidation pressure from agribusiness.
laws.penalty: Selling ALRO-reformed land: transaction void, land reverts to ALRO. Improper encroachment on forest land declared as agricultural: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Full title (Chanote) land freely transferable without restriction
Land purchased under land fund programs for small farmers has separate rules
Cooperative farming arrangements on ALRO land permitted

quiz.q: What restriction applies to land distributed to poor farmers under Thailand's ALRO land reform program?
options: Farmers must plant only crops designated by government
ALRO land cannot be sold — only inherited and farmed — preventing wealthy buyers from reconcentrating reformed land
Farmers must sell minimum 50% of production to government at fixed prices
ALRO land is leased not owned — farmers pay nominal annual rent
quiz.explanation: ALRO-distributed land cannot be sold — it can only be inherited within the family and must be used for farming. This anti-speculation restriction prevents wealthy buyers from acquiring poor farmers' newly reformed land. However, it also means farmers cannot use their land as loan collateral, limiting their ability to invest in improvements. This trade-off between security and economic utility is a classic land reform tension.
